kept.who: Han Yu · 'On the Teacher' (Shi Shuo 師說), c. 802, opening lines · tr. Shih Shun Liu, Renditions No. 8, Autumn 1977
kept.corrected_who: Han Yu 韓愈 (768–824) · 'On the Teacher' (Shi Shuo 師說), c. 802, opening paragraph · tr. Shih Shun Liu, Renditions No. 8 (Autumn 1977), Research Centre for Translation, CUHK
kept.corrected_quote: In ancient times scholars always had teachers. It takes a teacher to transmit the Way, impart knowledge and resolve doubts. Since man is not born with knowledge, who can be without doubt? But doubt will never be resolved without a teacher.
kept.original: 古之學者必有師。師者，所以傳道受業解惑也。人非生而知之者，孰能無惑？惑而不從師，其為惑也終不解矣。
kept.corrected_meaning: Long ago every learner had a teacher. No one is born knowing, and a teacher clears your doubts.
kept.evidence: I opened cuhk.edu.hk/rct/renditions/sample/b08.html ('On the Teacher, By Han Yu, Translated by Shih Shun Liu', Renditions No. 8, Autumn 1977). The first paragraph matches the quote word for word; the page prints 'IN ANCIENT TIMES' in small caps. I checked the Chinese against the raw zh.wikisource text of 師說 (from 全唐文 juan 558 and 古文觀止 juan 8), and it matches character for character. The other lines in the notes are also on the page: 'where the Way is, there is my teacher' and 'The pupil is therefore not necessarily inferior to the teacher...'. The page also confirms 'Li P'an, who is seventeen'. The c. 802 date is the usual one (Zhenyuan 18). It is not in used_quotes.txt. The translation is in copyright and the page says 'for researchers' personal use only', so use it as a short attributed quotation only.
kept.safety: Safe. The quote is about teachers and learning only. Leave out Han Yu's official career and his memorial against Buddhism (religious conflict). The essay's line about scholar-officials laughing at teachers is fine but not needed.

kept.who: Xuanzang (Hiuen-Tsiang), c. 602–664 · The Life of Hiuen-Tsiang by the Shaman Hwui Li, Book I p. 10 and Book III p. 107 · tr. Samuel Beal, 1888 (new ed. 1911, reissue 1914)
kept.corrected_who: Xuanzang (Hiuen-Tsiang), c. 602–664 · Huili, The Life of Hiuen-Tsiang, Book I p. 10 and Book III p. 107 · tr. Samuel Beal (1888; new ed. 1911, popular re-issue 1914, Kegan Paul). He left China in 629 (貞觀三年八月); Beal prints '630 A.D.' in error, and some scholars argue for 627.
kept.corrected_quote: The monk Xuanzang found China's teachers and books disagreed, so he went to India. At Nalanda he told the teacher Silabhadra: 'I am come from the country of China, desiring to learn from your instruction the principles of the Yoga-Sastra.'
kept.original: 莫知適從，乃誓遊西方以問所惑 (卷一) … 從支那國來，欲依師學《瑜伽論》。 (卷三)
kept.corrected_meaning: When his teachers disagreed, he travelled all the way to India to learn from the right teacher.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the archive.org full text of item b28983841. Its title page reads 'New Edition, 1911 / Popular Re-issue, 1914' with a preface by L. Cranmer-Byng. Book I, p. 10: 'each followed implicitly the teaching of his own school; but on verifying their doctrine he saw that the holy books differed much, so that he knew not which to follow. He then resolved to travel to the Western world in order to ask about doubtful passages.' The Fa-hien and Chi-yen line is on the same page. Book III, p. 107 (running head 'The Vision of Silabhadra'): 'I am come from the country of China, desiring to learn from your instruction the principles of the Yoga-Sastra.' This matches word for word. On p. 106 Beal calls the teacher 'Ching-fa-tsong... This is the same as Silabhadra', and the scene is at Nalanda. The Chinese matches zh.wikisource 大唐大慈恩寺三藏法師傳 卷01 and 卷03. Problem 1: the original story ran to 50 words, so I trimmed it to 40 without changing the quoted words. Problem 2: the date. Beal p. 11 converts 'the third year... of Chêng Kwan' to '630 A.D.', which is wrong; the Chinese 貞觀三年 is 629. I took the year out of the slide text to avoid a clash with the cited translation. The '5 years' claim in the notes is also in Beal: 'studied... during five years'. It is not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: The quoted lines are safe. The surrounding text has unsafe material, so keep all of it out: the imperial ban on travel ('an imperial rescript forbidding'), Silabhadra's illness and his wish to starve himself (told right after the quote on p. 107), the river bandits who tried to sacrifice him (Book III), and the kings. 'Yoga-Sastra' is the Buddhist Yogacarabhumi-sastra, not Patanjali and not asana. Any caption should call it a Buddhist text so no one thinks he went to learn asana.

kept.who: Luo Congyan 羅從彥 (1072–1135) · Song Shi (History of Song), juan 428, Biography of Luo Congyan, compiled 1343–45 · tr. own literal (no PD English found)
kept.corrected_who: Luo Congyan 羅從彥 (1072–1135) · as told in Song Shi (History of Song), juan 428 (Daoxue 2), biography of Luo Congyan, compiled 1343–45 · own literal translation (no published English found)
kept.corrected_quote: Luo Congyan walked to study with Yang Shi, who carried the Cheng brothers' teaching. Three days in, startled and soaked in sweat, he said: 'Had I not come here, I would nearly have wasted my whole life.'
kept.original: 聞同郡楊時得河南程氏學，慨然慕之……遂徒步往學焉。……從彥初見時三日，即驚汗浹背，曰：「不至是，幾虛過一生矣。」
kept.corrected_meaning: He walked to find a real teacher. Three days in, he knew he had nearly wasted his life.
kept.evidence: I opened the raw zh.wikisource text of 宋史/卷428, section 羅從彥. It reads: 聞同郡楊時得河南程氏學，慨然慕之，及時為蕭山令，遂徒步往學焉……從彥初見時三日，即驚汗浹背，曰：「不至是，幾虛過一生矣。」 The candidate's Chinese matches, with the ellipses in the right places. The follow-up in the notes is also there: 鬻田走洛，見頤問之……從彥謝曰：「聞之龜山具是矣。」乃歸卒業. Fix: the candidate's English dropped 驚 ('startled', i.e. the sweat came from shock), so I put it back. I also rendered 幾虛過一生 more literally as 'nearly wasted my whole life'. The new text is 37 words. The English is my own; no printed translation exists to check it against, so word_for_word is false, but the Chinese was checked character for character. This is an official dynastic-history anecdote, not a legend, but its timeline is muddled (Cheng Yi died 1107, before Yang Shi's Xiaoshan post), so give no date. It is not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: Safe as written. Leave out Luo's minor official post (惠州博羅縣主簿) and the fact that Yang Shi was magistrate of Xiaoshan. Also leave out the later parts of the biography: his political maxims about rulers and court, the 靖康 national crisis, and the An Lushan rebellion analogies.

kept.who: Song Lian 宋濂 (1310–1381) · Preface Seeing Off Ma Sheng of Dongyang (送東陽馬生序), c. 1378, para. 1 · tr. own literal (no PD English found)
kept.corrected_who: Song Lian 宋濂 (1310–1381) · 'Preface Seeing Off Ma Sheng of Dongyang' (送東陽馬生序), c. 1378, para. 1 · own literal translation from the zh.wikisource text (明文海 juan 285); no published English found
kept.corrected_quote: My family was poor... so I borrowed books from families who owned them, copied them out by hand, and returned them on the agreed day. In great cold the ink froze hard in the inkstone and my fingers could not bend or straighten, yet I did not slacken.
kept.original: 家貧，無從致書以觀，每假借於藏書之家，手自筆錄，計日以還。天大寒，硯冰堅，手指不可屈伸，弗之怠。
kept.corrected_meaning: Too poor to buy books, he copied borrowed ones by hand, even when the ink froze.
kept.evidence: I opened the raw zh.wikisource text of 送東陽馬生序 (from 明文海 四庫全書本 juan 285). Paragraph 1 has 家貧，無從致書以觀，每假借於藏書之家，手自筆錄，計日以還。天大寒，硯冰堅，手指不可屈伸，弗之怠, which matches the candidate's Chinese exactly. The '...' trim stands for 無從致書以觀 ('with no way to get books to read'). Fixes: 硯冰堅 is the ink frozen hard in the inkstone, and 屈伸 is 'bend or straighten', not just 'bend'. The other lines in the notes are also in the text: paragraph 2 has 嘗負箧曳屣 (the notes leave out 嘗 'once', a minor point) and 以中有足樂者. A web search found no published English translation, so word_for_word is false, but the Chinese was checked character for character. The c. 1378 date fits 余朝京師, his court visit after he retired in 1377. It is not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: The quoted lines are safe. Leave out the rest of the essay: 今雖耄老 (old age), 承天子之寵光 (imperial favour) and the Imperial Academy part. Also leave out his role as tutor at the Ming court, and his exile and death on the way, which followed a political purge.

kept.who: Yang Shi 楊時 (1053–1135) and You Zuo 游酢 at Cheng Yi's door · Song Shi juan 428, Biography of Yang Shi (1343–45); English in H. A. Giles, A Chinese Biographical Dictionary, 1898, pp. 912–913
kept.corrected_who: Yang Shi 楊時 (1053–1135) and You Zuo 游酢 with their teacher Cheng Yi 程頤 · Song Shi 宋史 juan 428 (Daoxue 2), Biography of Yang Shi, compiled 1343–45 · tr. own literal; cf. H. A. Giles, A Chinese Biographical Dictionary, 1898, pp. 912–913
kept.corrected_quote: One day Yang Shi and You Zuo visited their teacher Cheng Yi, who sat with eyes closed. They stood by him and did not leave; when he woke, the snow outside the door was a foot deep.
kept.original: 一日見頤，頤偶瞑坐，時與游酢侍立不去，頤既覺，則門外雪深一尺矣。
kept.corrected_meaning: Two students waited quietly for their teacher to wake, while a foot of snow fell outside.
kept.evidence: Opened zh.wikisource 宋史/卷428 (raw text). The Yang Shi biography has, word for word: 一日見頤，頤偶瞑坐，時與游酢侍立不去，頤既覺，則門外雪深一尺矣. It also confirms 時調官不赴 (he skipped an official post to study with Cheng Hao), 顥目送之曰：「吾道南矣。」 and 時蓋年四十矣 (about forty when he met Cheng Yi). Opened Giles 1898 on archive.org (chinesebiograph00gile, djvu text). The Yang Shih entry starts on p. 912 and runs onto p. 913: 'On one occasion, when the Master had dozed off, Yang Shih would not wake him, but remained standing at the door so long that a foot (some say three feet) of snow fell in the interval before the sleeper awaked.' The rest of the entry covers Wang An-shih and the 1126 peace, so leave that out as the notes say. Giles says he stayed with Cheng Yi 'until 1087', which does not fit Song Shi's age of forty, so leave out any year. The facts are right. The only change is a trim, because the original wording was 43 words and the limit is 40. The new version is 36 words. Not on the used list.
kept.safety: Safe. A teacher and his students, snow, and waiting. No politics if the Wang Anshi and 1126 treaty parts of Giles are left out. Do not show them standing out in the snow: in Song Shi they stand indoors at his side, and the snow piles up outside.

kept.who: Kuang Heng 匡衡 (1st c. BCE) · Xijing Zaji 西京雜記, juan 2 (anecdote collection, attrib. Liu Xin / Ge Hong) · tr. own literal; English summary in Giles, A Chinese Biographical Dictionary, 1898, no. 1011, p. 386
kept.corrected_who: Kuang Heng 匡衡 (1st c. BCE) · Xijing Zaji 西京雜記 juan 2 (anecdote collection, attributed to Liu Xin / Ge Hong) · tr. own literal; cf. H. A. Giles, A Chinese Biographical Dictionary, 1898, no. 1011, p. 386
kept.corrected_quote: The story goes that Kuang Heng studied hard but had no candles. A rich man in his town owned many books, so Kuang Heng worked for him unpaid. Asked why, he said: 'I wish to read all your books.'
kept.original: 匡衡字稚圭，勤學而無燭……邑人大姓文不識，家富多書，衡乃與其傭作，而不求償。主人怪，問衡，衡曰：「願得主人書遍讀之。」主人感歎，資給以書，遂成大學。
kept.corrected_meaning: Too poor for books, he worked for free just to read them, and became a great scholar.
kept.evidence: Opened zh.wikisource 西京雜記/卷二 (raw text). The passage matches the given original word for word, including 勤學而無燭, 邑人大姓文不識，家富多書, 衡乃與其傭作，而不求償, 「願得主人書遍讀之。」 and 遂成大學. The skipped middle (穿壁引其光, boring through the wall) is marked with an ellipsis. Opened Giles 1898 on archive.org. Entry no. 1011, K'uang Heng, is on p. 386: 'Born in poverty, he entered the service of a wealthy magnate as a menial and without wages, solely for the chance of being within reach of books.' The attribution is confirmed. Two fixes: 勤學 means 'studied hard', not 'loved study', and the text was trimmed from 42 to 39 words. 'The story goes' marks it as an old story, which is right for Xijing Zaji. Not on the used list.
kept.safety: Safe once the wall-boring half (鑿壁偷光) is left out, as done here. Do not mention his later career as a minister under Emperor Yuan (royalty and politics). 'Worked unpaid' is hired labour where he asked for no wages. It is not servitude.

kept.who: Che Yin 車胤 (d. c. 400) · Jin Shu 晉書 juan 83; Sun Kang 孫康 · Chuxue Ji 初學記 juan 2 citing Song Qi Yu 宋齊語; English in Giles, A Chinese Biographical Dictionary, 1898, no. 206 p. 87 and p. 692
kept.corrected_who: Che Yin 車胤 (4th c.) · Jin Shu 晉書 juan 83, Biography of Che Yin; Sun Kang 孫康 · Song Qi Yu 宋齊語 as cited in Chuxue Ji 初學記 juan 2 (Snow) · tr. own literal; cf. H. A. Giles, A Chinese Biographical Dictionary, 1898, no. 206 p. 87 and p. 692
kept.corrected_quote: Che Yin's family could not always afford lamp oil, so on summer nights he read by a bag of white silk holding dozens of fireflies. Another poor student, Sun Kang, read in winter by the light of the snow.
kept.original: 家貧不常得油，夏月則練囊盛數十螢火以照書，以夜繼日焉。(晉書·車胤傳)；孫康家貧，常映雪讀書。(初學記卷二引宋齊語)
kept.corrected_meaning: No money for lamp oil: one boy read by fireflies, another by snow light.
kept.evidence: Opened zh.wikisource 晉書/卷083. The Che Yin biography reads word for word: 家貧不常得油，夏月則練囊盛數十螢火以照書，以夜繼日焉. Opened zh.wikisource 初學記/卷第二 and 初學記 (四庫全書本)/卷02. The snow section has 《宋齊語》曰：孫康家貧，常映雪讀書. Opened Giles 1898 on archive.org. No. 206, Ch'e Yin, is on p. 87: 'too poor to afford a lamp, and studied by the light of a bag of fireflies.' Sun K'ang is on p. 692: 'so poor that he could not afford a lamp to read by. He therefore studied in winter by light reflected from the snow.' The text is 39 words, within the limit. Giles dates Che Yin's death '?397', and Jin Shu puts it in the Longan era (397–401), so the who line just says 4th century. Not on the used list.
kept.safety: Safe as written. Jin Shu confirms that Sima Yuanxian forced Che Yin to take his own life (元顯逼令自裁), so never mention how he died or his court career. Leave out Sun Kang's later post as a censor. Use only the boyhood study images.

kept.who: Confucius to his student Ran Qiu · Analects 6.10 (Legge numbering; 6.12 in modern editions) · tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1861 (rev. 1893)
kept.corrected_who: Confucius to his student Ran Qiu (Yen Ch'iu) · Analects Book VI, ch. 10 (Legge numbering; 6.12 in many modern editions) · tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1861 (rev. 1893)
kept.corrected_quote: Yen Ch'iu said, 'It is not that I do not delight in your doctrines, but my strength is insufficient.' The Master said, 'Those whose strength is insufficient give over in the middle of the way but now you limit yourself.'
kept.original: 冉求曰：「非不說子之道，力不足也。」子曰：「力不足者，中道而廢。今女畫。」
kept.corrected_meaning: A student said, 'I'm too weak.' The teacher said, 'The weak stop halfway. You stopped before starting.'
kept.evidence: Opened Project Gutenberg eBook #4094 (Legge, The Chinese Classics, Volume 1: Confucian Analects, plain text). Book VI, 'CHAP. X.' reads exactly: 'Yen Ch'iu said, 'It is not that I do not delight in your doctrines, but my strength is insufficient.' The Master said, 'Those whose strength is insufficient give over in the middle of the way but now you limit yourself.'' The Chinese below it ends 足者、中道而廢、今女畫. It matches word for word, and Legge has no comma before 'but now'. The used list has only Analects 11.21 about Ch'iu, which is a different passage, and nothing for 6.10/6.12. The meaning line was tightened, because Confucius's point is that the weak give up halfway while Ran Qiu drew his line before even trying.
kept.safety: Safe. A teacher talking with a student about effort. No politics, and Ran Qiu's later service to the Ji clan is not mentioned. Not an old-age line.

kept.who: Confucius · Analects 7.8 (Legge VII.8) · tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1861 (rev. 1893)
kept.corrected_who: Confucius · Analects 7.8 (Legge VII.8) · tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (1861; 2nd rev. ed. 1893)
kept.corrected_quote: I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge... When I have presented one corner of a subject to any one, and he cannot from it learn the other three, I do not repeat my lesson.
kept.original: 子曰：「不憤不啟，不悱不發。舉一隅不以三隅反，則不復也。」
kept.corrected_meaning: A teacher opens the door only for a keen student, who must work out the rest himself.
kept.evidence: Opened Gutenberg #4094 (Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, Confucian Analects). Book VII, CHAP. VIII reads: 'The Master said, 'I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge, nor help out any one who is not anxious to explain himself. When I have presented one corner of a subject to any one, and he cannot from it learn the other three, I do not repeat my lesson.'' The Chinese printed beside it is 【第八章】子曰、不憤不啟、不悱不發、舉一隅、不以三隅反、則不復也。 The trimmed quote matches word for word, and the '...' marks the removed clause. Legge's VII.8 is also 7.8 in modern numbering, because the numbers only split after VII.9. Safety is clean: no conflict, royalty or old age. It is not on used_quotes.txt; the Confucius lines there are 9.19, 13.17, 11.21, 17.2, 2.4 and the 'hundred efforts' line.
kept.safety: Clean. It is a teaching line with no conflict, politics, royalty or old age.

kept.who: Confucius · Analects 7.19 (Legge VII.19; 7.20 in modern editions) · tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1861 (rev. 1893)
kept.corrected_who: Confucius · Analects 7.20 (Legge VII.19) · tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1 (1861; 2nd rev. ed. 1893)
kept.corrected_quote: I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge; I am one who is fond of antiquity, and earnest in seeking it there.
kept.original: 子曰：「我非生而知之者，好古，敏以求之者也。」
kept.corrected_meaning: Even Confucius was not born knowing. He loved the old teachings and worked hard to seek them.
kept.evidence: Opened Gutenberg #4094 (Legge). Book VII, CHAP. XIX reads exactly: 'The Master said, 'I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge; I am one who is fond of antiquity, and earnest in seeking it there.'' The Chinese is 【十九章】子曰、我非生而知之者、好古、敏以求之者也。 Legge's VII.18 is the Duke of Sheh passage, which ends with 'does not perceive that old age is coming on'. That passage is modern 7.19, so the label must not lead with '7.19'. A web check confirms that standard modern numbering (Lau, Yang Bojun, ctext) puts this line at 7.20. Lapham's Quarterly cites it as VII.20. The fix only reorders the label to lead with the modern number 7.20; the quote text is unchanged. The extra option in the notes, Legge VII.21 'When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers...', is also verified verbatim in the same file (modern 7.22). It is not on used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: Clean. Use only VII.19 (modern 7.20). Do not use the neighbouring Legge VII.18 (modern 7.19), which ends with an old-age line.

kept.who: Song Lian 宋濂 (1310–1381) · Preface Seeing Off Ma Sheng of Dongyang (送東陽馬生序), c. 1378, para. 1 · tr. own literal (no PD English found)
kept.corrected_who: Song Lian 宋濂 (1310–1381) · Preface Seeing Off Ma Sheng of Dongyang (送東陽馬生序), para. 1 · own literal translation from the Chinese (no published public-domain English found)
kept.corrected_quote: I once hurried more than a hundred li to an honoured elder scholar of my home district, the classic in my hands, to ask him questions... If he scolded me, I grew more respectful... I waited until he was pleased, then asked again. So, though I was slow, in the end I gained some learning.
kept.original: 嘗趨百里外，從鄉之先達執經叩問。……或遇其叱咄，色愈恭，禮愈至，不敢出一言以復；俟其欣悅，則又請焉。故余雖愚，卒獲有所聞。
kept.corrected_meaning: He walked far to a teacher, took scolding with respect, kept asking, and in the end he learned.
kept.evidence: Opened zh.wikisource 送東陽馬生序 (from 明文海, 四庫全書本, 卷285). Paragraph 1 has every Chinese clause in the 'original' field, word for word: 嘗趨百里外，從鄉之先達執經叩問。先達德隆望尊……余立侍左右，援疑質理，俯身傾耳以請；或遇其叱咄，色愈恭，禮愈至，不敢出一言以復；俟其欣悅，則又請焉。故余雖愚，卒獲有所聞。 No published English translation could be found (web search came up empty), so the quote cannot be word for word with a printed translation. It is an own literal rendering and must be labelled that way. Three wording fixes bring it closer to the Chinese. (1) 俟其欣悅 means 'I waited until he was pleased'; the old 'pleased again' added a word that is not in the source. (2) 卒獲有所聞 means 'in the end I gained some learning'; 'I came to learn' overstated it. (3) 鄉之先達 means 'an accomplished elder of my home district'; 'honoured' rests on the next phrase, 德隆望尊. The second '...' now also marks the omitted 不敢出一言以復. The 'c. 1378' date is the usual textbook dating, and the text itself says 余朝京師. However, no source found in this check confirms the year, so it was removed from the attribution. Song Lian's dates of 1310–1381 match Wikipedia and Britannica. It is not on used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: The excerpt is clean. Being scolded is not violence. Paragraph 2 of the full essay mentions the emperor's favour (承天子之寵光), Song's old age (耄老) and the court, so quote only paragraph 1. Do not mention Song Lian's court career or his later exile.

kept.who: Faxian (Fa-Hien) · A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms, ch. 1, ch. 36 and closing account · tr. James Legge, 1886
kept.corrected_who: Faxian (Fa-Hien) · A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms, ch. I, ch. XXXVI and closing envoy (Faxian's words as reported by the envoy's writer) · tr. James Legge, Oxford, 1886
kept.corrected_quote: In 399 the monk Faxian left China for India to find the full rules for monks, then spent three years in Pataliputra copying them. He said: '...I had a definite aim, and thought of nothing but to do my best...'
kept.original: 法顯本求戒律，而北天竺諸國皆師師口傳，無本可寫……故法顯住此三年，學梵書、梵語，寫律。／蓋是志有所存，專其愚直
kept.corrected_meaning: He spent fifteen years travelling to bring the full rules home, because his aim was clear.
kept.evidence: Opened Gutenberg #2124 (Legge, A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms; preface signed 'Oxford: June, 1886'). Ch. I: Faxian, 'Deploring the mutilated and imperfect state of the collection of the Books of Discipline', set out to 'seek for the Disciplinary Rules'. Legge's note 2 dates the start to A.D. 399; zh.wikisource 佛國記 has 弘始二年歲在己亥, and 己亥 is 399. Ch. XXXVI ('IN PATNA... INDIAN STUDIES FOR THREE YEARS') says he found 'one master transmitting orally (the rules) to another, but no written copies which he could transcribe' and 'stayed here for three years, learning Sanskrit books and the Sanskrit speech, and writing out the Vinaya rules' at Pataliputtra. The closing account gives 'six years to reach Central India; stoppages there extended over (other) six years; and on his return it took him three years', which is 15 years. In the envoy, which Legge says is by 'another hand', the writer reports: 'He said himself, '...was because I had a definite aim, and thought of nothing but to do my best in my simplicity and straightforwardness.'' The quoted words are verbatim; the trim removes 'That I encountered danger and trod the most perilous places...' before them. The Chinese was checked on zh.wikisource 佛國記: 無本可寫, 故法顯住此三年，學梵書、梵語，寫律, and 蓋是志有所存，專其愚直 all match. The candidate text was about 50 words, so it was cut to 40 to fit the limit. It is not on used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: The story as cut is clean: a monk travels to learn and copy texts. Leave out the danger and death in the rest of his sentence ('exposed my life where death seemed inevitable'), the dry bones of the dead in the desert, the storms at sea, the kings and prefects, and his age. The book title's word 'Kingdoms' is only a title and does not put royalty in the content.

kept.who: Huineng 慧能 (638–713) · Platform Sutra (Zongbao ed.), ch. 1 'Autobiography' · based on tr. Wong Mou-lam 1930, ed. Dwight Goddard, A Buddhist Bible, 1932/1938, pp. 220–221
kept.corrected_who: Huineng 慧能 (638–713) · Platform Sutra (Zongbao ed., Taisho T2008), ch. 1 行由品 'Autobiography of Hui-Neng' · Wong Mou-lam's translation (Yu Ching Press, Shanghai, 1930), as edited by Dwight Goddard, A Buddhist Bible, 1st ed. 1932, pp. 220–221
kept.corrected_quote: The story goes that Huineng, a poor firewood seller from the south, travelled about thirty days to the Fifth Patriarch and said, 'I ask for nothing but Buddhahood.' He then split firewood and hulled rice for over eight months.
kept.original: 惠能安置母畢，即便辭違。不經三十餘日，便至黃梅，禮拜五祖……惟求作佛，不求餘物……差惠能破柴踏碓。經八月餘
kept.corrected_meaning: He travelled a month to meet his teacher, then chopped wood and pounded rice for over eight months.
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com/bud/bb/bb26.htm is behind a Cloudflare check, so I read it through the web.archive.org copy and the neonvagabond.xyz mirror. Both are the same page: A Buddhist Bible, Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, Chapter I. On p. 220 Huineng says he was 'selling firewood in the market' after his family was left 'poor', and 'I left for Wong-mui which took me about thirty days to reach'. On p. 221 he says, word for word, "I ask for nothing but Buddhahood.", then that he 'was told by a lay brother to split firewood and hull rice', and 'More than eight months after the Patriarch met me one day...'. The sacred-texts index says this e-text is the FIRST EDITION (1932, self-published in Vermont). The 1938 Dutton edition is a different, enlarged book with different page numbers, so pp. 220–221 belong to the 1932 edition only, and I removed '/1938'. The preface on p. 217 says the version is 'based upon' Wong Mou-lam's translation published by the Yu Ching Press, Shanghai. I checked the Chinese against CBETA T2008 (Zongbao ed., juan 1), fetched through cbdata.dila.edu.tw. It matches exactly: 惠能安置母畢，即便辭違。不經三十餘日，便至黃梅，禮拜五祖…惟求作佛，不求餘物…有一行者，差惠能破柴踏碓。經八月餘. FIXES: (1) 'walked' is not in the source. Neither the Chinese (便至黃梅, 'reached Huangmei') nor Goddard says how he travelled, so it now says 'travelled'. Same fix in the meaning line. (2) The candidate story was 45 words, so I trimmed it to 39 by cutting 'far' and folding the work and the eight months into one clause. (3) The edition and year are now set to the 1932 first edition. 'The story goes' stays as the legend label, since this biography is hagiography. Not in used_quotes.txt: I searched for Huineng, Hui, Neng, Patriarch, Platform, 六祖, 黃梅, Buddhahood, firewood and rice, with no matches.
kept.safety: Safe as corrected. It is about a teacher and a student, with hard work and no conflict. LEAVE OUT the father's banishment and early death, the Patriarch calling him an 'aborigine'/獦獠 (both a slur and mocking), the line 'lest evil men should harm you' (恐有惡人害汝), and the Patriarch's later words about seeing one's nature 'even if he were engaged in a battle' (輪刀上陣). Also leave out the later night flight with the robe and the monks who chased him, which is outside this excerpt. The Fifth Patriarch is a monastery abbot, not royalty. Optional extra line, verbatim from p. 221: 'Although there are Northern men and Southern men, but North or South make no difference in their Buddha-nature.' Use only that first sentence, because the next one repeats 'aboriginee'.

kept.corrected_quote: In 1859 Fukuzawa couldn't read Yokohama's shop signs: 'On the very next day... I took up a new aim in my life.' He walked five miles to a teacher who never taught him, so 'day and night I plodded along.'
kept.corrected_meaning: His old skills were not enough, so he started again the next day and kept going, even without a teacher.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the djvu full text of the archive.org scan (in.ernet.dli.2015.172747). The title page reads: Translated by Eiichi Kiyooka, Introduction by Shinzo Koizumi, The Hokuseido Press, 1934. Chapter V is headed 'LEARNING ENGLISH', with running heads on pp. 103-111. kept.corrected_who: Dogen · Bendowa (弁道話, 1231), tr. Norman Waddell and Abe Masao, 'Dogen's Bendowa', The Eastern Buddhist n.s. 4.1 (1971), p. 130
kept.corrected_quote: After the desire to seek the Way awakened in me, I went to all parts of the country, calling upon religious teachers... In addition, I proceeded to great Sung China, where I visited some of the leading priests... Ultimately, I went to Tai-pai peak and engaged in religious practice under the Zen master Ju-ching...
kept.original: 予、発心求法よりこのかた、わが朝の遍方に知識をとぶらひき。…予かさねて大宋国におもむき、知識を両浙にとぶらひ、家風を五門にきく。つひに大白峰の浄禅師に参じて、一生参学の大事ここにをはりぬ。
kept.corrected_meaning: He searched his whole country for teachers, then went to China, until he found the right one.
kept.evidence: I opened the Otani repository PDF (EB4-1-09.pdf). On printed page 130 it reads: 'After the desire to seek the Way awakened in me, I went to all parts of the country, calling upon religious teachers, until I chanced to encounter the priest Myozen of Kennin-ji...' and 'In addition, I proceeded to great Sung China, where I visited some of the leading priests of Liang-che, and learned of the different characteristics of the Five Gates. Both quoted sentences are on p.130, not pp.129-130. Page 129 is the earlier 'This Dharma is amply present...' passage. Footnote 19 identifies Tai-pai feng as another name for the T'ien-t'ung (Tiantong) monastery complex. I added the 'great Sung China' line because the meaning line names China. I checked the Japanese against the SAT Taisho database (T2582, 82.15): 予發心求法ヨリコノカタ。ワカ朝ノ遍方ニ知識ヲトフラヒキ。…予カサネテ大宋國ニオモムキ。知識ヲ兩浙ニトフラヒ。家風ヲ五門ニキク。ツヒニ大白峯ノ淨禪師ニ參シテ。一生參學ノ大事ココニヲハリヌ。 The ne.jp page has the same words in hiragana with 大白峰. The candidate's Japanese was right but skipped the China sentence.
kept.safety: Safe. Do not bring in the translators' introduction about Mt. Hiei monks threatening Dogen, or Myozen's death in China. Note that another Bendowa line (Waddell/Abe p.129, 'This Dharma is amply present in every person...') is already in used_quotes.txt. This is a different passage, so it is not a duplicate, but it is the same work.

kept.who: Hwang Sang · Imsul-gi (壬戌記, 1862), recalling his teacher Jeong Yak-yong (Dasan) in October 1802; Korean tr. Ahn Dae-hoe, Kyunghyang Shinmun, 7 June 2002; English is a plain rendering from that Korean
kept.corrected_who: Hwang Sang · Imsul-gi (壬戌記, 1862), recalling his teacher Jeong Yak-yong (Dasan) in 1802; Korean tr. Ahn Dae-hoe, Kyunghyang Shinmun, 7 June 2002 (English is our plain rendering of the Korean; no published English translation found)
kept.corrected_quote: In 1802, 15-year-old Hwang Sang told his teacher Jeong Yak-yong he was dull, blocked and slow. 'The way to dig in? Diligence. To break through? Diligence. To polish? Diligence,' came the answer, and Hwang kept it sixty years.
kept.original: 파고드는 방법은 무엇이냐. 근면함이다. 뚫는 방법은 무엇이냐. 근면함이다. 닦는 방법은 무엇이냐. 근면함이다.
kept.corrected_meaning: A boy thought he was too slow to learn. His teacher said the way is hard work, again and again.
kept.evidence: I opened the Kyunghyang 2002 article ('공부의 자세, 황상의 壬戌記', by Ahn Dae-hoe). The Korean line '파고드는 방법은 무엇이냐. 근면함이다. 뚫는 방법은 무엇이냐. 근면함이다. 닦는 방법은 무엇이냐. 근면함이다.' appears exactly. The boy's words are '제가 병통 세가지가 있어서요. 첫째는 둔하고, 둘째는 꽉 막혔고, 셋째는 미욱합니다' ('I have three faults: dull, blocked, dim'). He said this when the teacher urged him to study, not 'too ... to study'. The memoir says: '나는 나이 15세 소년' and '마음에 새기고 뼈에 새겨... 그날로부터 지금까지 60여년의 세월이 흘렀다', written in the 임술 year 1862. I also opened the Kyunghyang 2017 review of Jeong Min's book. It confirms that Hwang Sang (1788-1870) bowed to Dasan and that seven days later, on 17 October 1802, Dasan gave him the note 贈山石. Age 15 is East Asian reckoning, about 14 in Western years. I found no classical Chinese original and no published English translation, so the English is a faithful rendering, not a printed translation (word_for_word false). I trimmed the story to the 40-word limit and made the dialogue closer to the Korean ('What is the way to dig in? Diligence').
kept.safety: Keep the exile out. Dasan was in Gangjin as a banished 'serious criminal' after the 1801 Catholic persecution, which is politics and religious conflict, so mention neither. Also leave out Hwang's age (75) at writing and his father's job as a clerk. As trimmed, the story is safe. Not in used_quotes.txt.

kept.who: Kukai · Shorai mokuroku (御請来目録, his report on the texts he brought home, 806), tr. in Wm. Theodore de Bary et al., Sources of Japanese Tradition (Columbia UP, 1958), pp. 144-46
kept.corrected_who: Kukai · Shorai mokuroku (御請来目録, 806; Taisho T2161, 55.1065a), tr. in Ryusaku Tsunoda, Wm. Theodore de Bary and Donald Keene (comp.), Sources of Japanese Tradition (Columbia UP, 1958), pp. 144-46

kept.original: 我先知汝來。相待久矣。今日相見大好大好。
kept.corrected_meaning: He went from teacher to teacher far from home, and one teacher had been waiting for him.
kept.evidence: I fetched SAT T2161 (御請來目録) at 55.1065a. It reads: 二十四年仲春十一日。大使等旋軔本朝。唯空海孑然...留住西明寺...於是歴城中訪名徳。偶然奉遇青龍寺東塔院和尚法諱惠果阿闍梨...和尚乍見含笑。喜歡告曰。我先知汝來。相待久矣。今日相見大好大好。報命欲竭... Enryaku 24 is 805. kept.safety: Safe as trimmed. Cut 'His teachings were lofty enough to guide emperors. Three sovereigns revered him' (royalty), 'My life is drawing to an end' (death or old age), the envoy and court framing, and the 804 sea crossing with lost ships. Not in used_quotes.txt.

kept.who: Dogen · Gakudo Yojinshu (学道用心集, c. 1234), section 5 'To practice Zazen and study the truth, look for a true master', tr. Gudo Wafu Nishijima
kept.corrected_who: Dogen · Gakudo Yojinshu (学道用心集, c. 1234), section 5 'To practice Zazen and study the truth, look for a true master', tr. Gudo Nishijima
kept.corrected_quote: The student is like a fine wood and the master is like a carpenter. Quality wood will not show its beauty unless it is in the hands of a good carpenter.
kept.original: 機は良材の如く、師は工匠に似たり。縦い良材たりといえども、良工を得ざれば奇麗未だ彰われず。
kept.corrected_meaning: A good student is like good wood: it needs a good teacher's hands to show its beauty.

kept.who: Dogen · Tenzo Kyokun (典座教訓, 1237), tr. Thomas Wright, in Kosho Uchiyama, How to Cook Your Life (Shambhala 2005; first published Weatherhill 1983)
kept.corrected_who: Dogen · Tenzo Kyokun (典座教訓, 1237), tr. Thomas Wright, in Dogen and Kosho Uchiyama, How to Cook Your Life (Shambhala 2005; first published Weatherhill 1983)
kept.corrected_quote: In China in 1223, Dogen met a tenzo (temple cook) who laughed: 'You do not yet understand what practice is all about...' Dogen wrote: 'Whatever little bit I have learned about characters and practice is largely due to that tenzo.'
kept.original: 外国の好人、未だ辨道を了得せず、未だ文字を知得せざること在り … 山僧聊か文字を知り、辨道を了するは、乃ち彼の典座の大恩なり
kept.corrected_meaning: A young monk travelled far to learn, and a temple cook showed him what practice really is.
kept.evidence: I opened the terebess PDF of How to Cook Your Life, translated by Thomas Wright. The copyright page says 'Originally published: New York: Weatherhill, 1983', and the LoC data gives 2005. Pages 29 to 31 say Dogen arrived in China in April 1223 and was staying on board ship at Ningbo. 'One day in May' the tenzo from Mount Ayuwang came to the ship to buy mushrooms; asked 'Is it far from here?' he answered 'About fourteen miles.' Then: 'He burst out laughing and remarked, "My good friend from abroad! You do not yet understand what practice is all about, nor do you know the meaning of characters."' In July the tenzo visited Dogen at Mount Tiantong. Then: 'Whatever little bit I have learned about characters and practice is largely due to that tenzo.' Both quotes are exact; trims are marked with .... Corrections: (1) I cut the story to 40 words. (2) The source never says the cook 'walked'. It only gives the distance, so I removed 'walked'. (3) The Japanese reading with 辨 (a variant of 辦) comes from the Antaiji study notes, which I saw only as a search excerpt and did not check against a critical edition. The 'largely due' line is the standard reading. The 'One, two, three, four, five' / 'There is nothing in the world that is hidden' exchange is verified on p. 31 and can be a second slide. Not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: Safe as corrected. Leave out the cook's age (about sixty, sixty-one), 'in my old age' and 'when you are so old', because of the old-age rule. Also leave out Myozen, who 'later died in China'. None of these are in the corrected text.

kept.who: Japanese proverb, origin unknown · cited and explained by Prof. Imamura (今村健志), Ehime University, column 'Kokoro ni nokoru hitokoto' (2023)
kept.corrected_who: Japanese proverb (origin unknown); listed in the proverb dictionaries Kotowaza no Mori (proverb.jp) and Kotowaza Kanyoku no Hyakka Jiten, and cited by Prof. Takeshi Imamura (今村健志), Vice-President, Ehime University (2023)
kept.corrected_quote: Rather than spend three years studying hard, better to spend three years choosing a teacher.
kept.original: 三年勤め学ばんよりは三年師を選ぶべし
kept.corrected_meaning: Finding the right teacher matters more than years of studying on your own.
kept.evidence: Kotobank and Weblio have no entry; Weblio returned a 'no match' page, and kotowaza-allguide is blocked from here. I did find it in several other places. kept.safety: Safe. A proverb about choosing a teacher, with no sensitive content.

kept.who: Sugita Genpaku · Rangaku Kotohajime (蘭学事始, 1815); English is a plain rendering from the Japanese (published tr. Ryozo Matsumoto, Dawn of Western Science in Japan, Hokuseido 1969)
kept.corrected_who: Sugita Genpaku · Rangaku Kotohajime (蘭学事始, 1815). English is a plain rendering from the Japanese text on Japanese Wikisource (published English tr. Ryozo Matsumoto, Dawn of Western Science in Japan, Hokuseido Press 1969)
kept.corrected_quote: In 1771 Sugita Genpaku and friends began translating a Dutch anatomy book with no real dictionary. One line, 'the eyebrow is hair that grows above the eye', puzzled them until sunset, yet their translation came out in 1774.
kept.original: 譬へば眉といふものは、目の上に生じたる毛なりと有るやうなる一句、彷彿として長き日の春の一日には明らめられず、日暮る迄考へ詰め
kept.corrected_meaning: With no dictionary, even one easy sentence puzzled them all day, but they kept going.
kept.evidence: I opened the rendered page 蘭學事始 on ja.wikisource, which is transcluded from 文明源流叢書. The header gives 文化十二 / 1815. These lines are all verified. 誠に艫舵なき船の大海に乘出せしが如く、茫洋として寄べきなく. 翁いまだ二十五字さえ習はず (the leader is 良澤, 先生とも仰ぐ事となしぬ). 譬へば眉といふものは、目の上に生じたる毛なりと有るやうなる一句、彷彿として長き日の春の一日には明らめられず、日暮る迄考へ詰め、互ににらみ合て…一行も解し得る事ならぬ. 其頃ウオールデンブツク〈釋辭書〉といふものもなし (only a small booklet Ryotaku brought from Nagasaki, hence 'no real dictionary'). 連城の玉をも得し心地せり, said of the word フルへツヘンド. The book acquisition is dated 明和八年 (1771), and the reading began 其翌日 at Ryotaku's house. Nakagawa Jun'an and others were also there, so I wrote 'and friends'. Kaitai Shinsho was published in 安永3 (1774), confirmed by Kotobank 解体新書 and NDL Nichiran. The Matsumoto/Hokuseido 1969 translation is confirmed by library catalogues. Corrections: (1) I cut the story from about 75 words to 38. (2) The source says the eyebrow line could NOT be worked out in a long spring day, even after thinking until dark. So 'took them a whole day' (which implies they solved it) became 'puzzled them until sunset'. (3) The English inside the quote marks is our own rendering, not Matsumoto's printed text. Alternative line for another slide: 'like setting out on a great ocean in a ship without oar or rudder' (誠に艫舵なき船の大海に乘出せしが如く).
kept.safety: Safe as corrected. Never mention the dissection the day before at Kotsukappara (an executed criminal), the 'eta' dissector, or the passages about companions who died young. None of these are in the corrected text.

kept.corrected_quote: In 1850s Osaka, student Fukuzawa Yukichi's pillow was nowhere to be found: 'I realized suddenly that I had not used one for the whole year... I had been studying without regard to day or night, rest or relaxation.'
kept.corrected_meaning: He studied day and night for a whole year and never once slept on a pillow.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the archive.org djvu text of the 1934 Hokuseido edition. The title page reads 'Translated by Eiichi Kiyooka... The Hokuseido Press 1934', and the contents list 'IV. The page goes on: 'I had gone through the year without ever spreading my pallet and covers and sleeping on the pillow' and 'In this I was not unusual or more studious than the others; all my friends lived in this way.' Fact fix: he asked for the pillow in his brother's rooms at the domain's Osaka headquarters, not in the school. I also cut the quote to 40 words. kept.original: श्रद्धावाँल्लभते ज्ञानं तत्परः संयतेन्द्रियः । ज्ञानं लब्ध्वा परां शान्तिमचिरेणाधिगच्छति ॥ (BhG 4.39)
kept.corrected_meaning: Trust, control yourself, and give your whole heart to it. Then you will learn, and peace comes soon.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the archive.org OCR text of item wg908 (metadata: '1882 - The Sacred Books Of East Vol 8', creator Kashinath Trimbak Telang). Page 62 ends 'He who has faith, whose' and page 63 (running head 'CHAPTER V, 3') goes on 'senses are restrained, and who is assiduous, obtains knowledge [fn 1]. Obtaining knowledge, he acquires, without delay, the highest tranquillity.' Telang prints the Gita as continuous prose, and this comes just after 'That you should learn by salutation, question, and service' (4.34), so the verse is 4.39. The quote is word for word, pp. 62–63. GRETIL Bhagavadgita-4comm reads 'śraddhāvāṃl labhate jñānaṃ tatparaḥ saṃyatendriyaḥ | jñānaṃ labdhvā parāṃ śāntim acireṇādhigacchati ||39||', so the Devanagari and the verse number are correct. Gita 4.39 is not in used_quotes.txt (the Gita lines used so far are 2.47, 5.27, 6.23–25, 6.35 and 6.40-ish Arnold).
kept.safety: Safe. The Gita is spoken on a battlefield, but this line has no war, conflict or violence in it, and Gita lines have already run in the series. Do not quote what comes next ('destroy, with the sword of knowledge...').

kept.corrected_quote: It’s not just Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith, energy, mindfulness, immersion, and wisdom; I too have these things. Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching...?
kept.original: na kho āḷārasseva kālāmassa atthi saddhā, mayhampatthi saddhā; ... vīriyaṁ ... sati ... samādhi ... paññā, mayhampatthi paññā. Yannūnāhaṁ yaṁ dhammaṁ āḷāro kālāmo ... pavedeti, tassa dhammassa sacchikiriyāya padaheyyan (MN 26:15.15–20)
kept.corrected_meaning: My teacher has trust, effort and focus. So do I. Why not work hard and learn it too?
kept.evidence: I fetched the SuttaCentral bilara API (mn26/sujato). The segments read: 15.15 'It’s not just Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith,' 15.16 'energy,' 15.17 'mindfulness,' 15.18 'immersion,' 15.19 'and wisdom; I too have these things.' 15.20 'Why don’t I make an effort to realize the same teaching that Āḷāra Kālāma says he has realized with his own insight?' The quote is word for word, the end of 15.20 is trimmed and marked with '...', and the Pali root text matches. The story context checks out too: 15.2 'Reverend Kālāma, I wish to lead the spiritual life in this teaching and training'; §16 Uddaka son of Rāma; and 17.1 'Traveling stage by stage in the Magadhan lands, I arrived at the town of Senā in Uruvelā.' kept.safety: Safe as quoted. If you tell the story, leave out the parents weeping, Āḷāra's death, and 15.35–36 ('this teaching was inadequate, I left disappointed'), so it does not read as putting down a teacher. Keep the point on his own effort.

kept.who: Bhrigu and his father-teacher Varuna · Taittiriya Upanishad III.1–6 (Bhrigu Valli), tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15, 1884, pp. 64–66
kept.corrected_who: Bhrigu and his father Varuna · Taittiriya Upanishad III (Bhrigu Valli), Anuvakas 1–6, tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1884), pp. 64–66
kept.corrected_quote: The Upanishad tells that Bhrigu went to his father Varuna, saying: 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' Four times he came back asking and was told, 'Try to know Brahman by penance...', and each time he practised, until he understood.
kept.original: भृगुर्वै वारुणिः । वरुणं पितरमुपससार । अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति । ... तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व । तपो ब्रह्मेति ॥
kept.corrected_meaning: He kept going back to ask his teacher. The answer was: practise hard, and you will find out.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the archive.org OCR of wg915 ('1884 - The Sacred Books Of East Vol 15 ... The Upanishads Part 2', Max Muller) and checked it against a local copy of the same edition. Third Valli, 'Or, the Chapter of Bhrigu', starts on p. 64: 'Bhrigu Vâruni went to his father Varuna, saying: "Sir, teach me Brahman."' In the first Anuvaka the answer is NOT about penance: 'Food, breath, the eye, the ear, mind, speech' and 'That from whence these beings are born... try to know that. That is Brahman.' In Anuvakas 2–5 (pp. 64–65) he 'went again to his father Varuna' and was told 'Try to know Brahman by penance, for penance is (the means of knowing) Brahman.' That makes 5 requests, 4 penance answers and 4 returns. Each Anuvaka ends 'He performed penance.' In the 6th (p. 66) 'He perceived that bliss is Brahman.' The candidate had two errors, both fixed: 'Each time the answer was penance' (wrong for the first time) and 'five times... came back' (he came back four times). In the Sanskrit Wikisource Bhriguvalli text, 'अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति' appears 5 times and 'तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व' 4 times.
kept.safety: Safe. It is scripture, labelled 'The Upanishad tells'. Varuna (a Vedic god) is shown respectfully, as father and teacher. Avoid the refrain 'into that they enter at their death'. A slide can gloss penance as [tapas].

kept.who: Uddalaka to his son Svetaketu · Chandogya Upanishad VI.14.1–2, tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 1 (The Upanishads Part I), 1879, pp. 105–106
kept.corrected_who: Uddalaka Aruni to his son Svetaketu · Chandogya Upanishad VI.14.2, tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 1 (The Upanishads, Part I), Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1879, p. 106 (parable starts VI.14.1, p. 105)
kept.corrected_quote: ...he would by asking his way from village to village arrive at last at Gandhâra,—in exactly the same manner does a man, who meets with a teacher to inform him, obtain the true knowledge.
kept.original: स ग्रामाद्ग्रामं पृच्छन्पण्डितो मेधावी गन्धारानेवोपसम्पद्येतैवमेवेहाचार्यवान्पुरुषो वेद
kept.corrected_meaning: A teacher points the way home, but you still walk it yourself, asking at every village.
kept.evidence: Opened the Wikisource proofread transcription of SBE vol. 1 (Khândogya-upanishad, Sixth Prapâthaka, Fourteenth Khanda), which is based on the 1879 Clarendon scan. Verse 2 reads: 'And as thereupon some one might loose his bandage and say to him, "Go in that direction, it is Gandhâra, go in that direction;" and as thereupon, having been informed and being able to judge for himself, he would by asking his way from village to village arrive at last at Gandhâra,—in exactly the same manner does a man, who meets with a teacher to inform him, obtain the true knowledge[30].' The quoted section matches word for word, including Müller's ',—'. Page anchors put the start of VI.14.1 on p. 105 and the quoted words on p. 106. The speaker is the father, named in VI.1.1 as 'Uddâlaka, the son of Aruna'. Footnote 30 is Shankara's gloss, which adds robbers and a forest of tigers. Müller's main text has no robbers, as the notes say. The Sanskrit fragment matches VI.14.2 (sa grāmād grāmaṃ pṛcchan paṇḍito medhāvī gandhārān evopasampadyeta evam evehācāryavān puruṣo veda). The archive.org item in.ernet.dli.2015.893 is 'The Sacred Books of the East Vol-i (1879)', Müller, Clarendon Press. I also checked the Stage 2 side fact in VI.1.2 on p. 92: 'Having begun his apprenticeship (with a teacher) when he was twelve years of age, Svetaketu returned to his father, when he was twenty-four, having then studied all the Vedas,—conceited, considering himself well-read, and stern.' I could not open the sacred-texts.com mirror because of a Cloudflare block, so that link is unverified but not needed. The line is not in used_quotes.txt.
kept.safety: The quote is safe as trimmed. Do not use the opening of the parable in VI.14.1, where a man is led away blindfolded and left where there are no people, because it reads as an abduction. Never use Shankara's version in footnote 30, which has robbers and tigers (crime). If the Svetaketu ages are used on another slide, leave out the word 'conceited' so the sage is not mocked. Nothing about war, royalty, politics or old age.

kept.who: Yama to Nachiketas · Katha Upanishad I.2.7–9, tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15, 1884, p. 9
kept.corrected_who: Yama (called 'Death' in Müller's text) to Nachiketas · Katha Upanishad I.2.7–9, tr. F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (The Upanishads, Part II), Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1884, p. 9
kept.corrected_quote: ...wonderful is a man, when found, who is able to teach him (the Self)... unless it be taught by another, there is no way to it... thou art truly a man of true resolve. May we have always an inquirer like thee!
kept.original: आश्चर्यो वक्ता कुशलोऽस्य लब्धा ... अनन्यप्रोक्ते गतिरत्र नास्ति ... सत्यधृतिर्बतासि त्वादृङ्नो भूयान्नचिकेतः प्रष्टा ॥
kept.corrected_meaning: A good teacher is rare and you need one. A teacher hopes for a student with a strong will.
kept.evidence: Opened the Wikisource transcription of SBE vol. 15, Katha-upanishad, First Adhyâya, Second Vallî. Verse 7: '...wonderful is a man, when found, who is able to teach him (the Self); wonderful is he who comprehends him, when taught by an able teacher.' Verse 8: '...unless it be taught by another, there is no way to it, for it is inconceivably smaller than what is small.' Verse 9: '...Thou hast obtained it now; thou art truly a man of true resolve. May we have always an inquirer like thee!' All three pieces match word for word, and the trims are marked with '...'. Page anchors put verses 7 to 9 on p. 9. In Müller's text the speaker is labelled 'Death said:', and verse I.1.5 glosses him as 'Yama (the ruler of the departed)'. Footnote 26 is as the notes describe: 'Unless no is negative, for Yama, at first, does not like to communicate his knowledge.' Footnote 23 gives other readings of 'unless it be taught by another'. Müller's main text uses the reading quoted. The Sanskrit fragments match Katha 1.2.7, 1.2.8 and 1.2.9. The archive.org item wg915 is '1884 - The Sacred Books Of East Vol 15 ... The Upanishads Part 2', by Max Muller. Neither this line nor the Vivekananda 'awake, arise' line (Katha I.3.14) clashes: used_quotes.txt has only the Vivekananda paraphrase, which is a different verse.
kept.safety: The quote is safe on its own. The frame story is not. In I.1.4 the angry father says 'I shall give thee unto Death', and Müller notes the father 'had to be true to his word and to sacrifice his son'. The boy then waits three nights at Death's house without food. Never tell that frame or show it on screen. Call the speaker 'the teacher Yama' and do not stress 'Death'. Leave out verse 8's 'taught by an inferior man' (already cut) and the 'Be (king)' offer in I.1.24. Nothing about war, politics, crime or old age.

kept.who: Zeno of Citium · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII.2-4, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb), 1925
kept.corrected_who: Zeno of Citium (c. 334-262 BCE) · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII.2-4, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb vol. II), 1925
kept.corrected_quote: Zeno of Cyprus, then thirty, read about Socrates in an Athens bookshop and asked where such men could be found. Crates passed by, and the bookseller said, "Follow yonder man"; Zeno studied with teachers for twenty years.
kept.corrected_meaning: He asked where a real teacher was. When one walked by, he followed, and kept learning for twenty years.
kept.evidence: Opened the Wikisource raw text of Hicks, Book VII. VII.2-3 reads: 'He went up into Athens and sat down in a bookseller's shop, being then a man of thirty. As he went on reading the second book of Xenophon's Memorabilia, he was so pleased that he inquired where men like Socrates were to be found. Crates passed by in the nick of time, so the bookseller pointed to him and said, "Follow yonder man." From that day he became Crates's pupil.' VII.4: 'But at last he left Crates, and the men above mentioned were his masters for twenty years' (those men are Crates, Stilpo, Xenocrates and Polemo, VII.2). The quoted words 'Follow yonder man' are word for word. Fixes: (1) the draft ran about 65 words, now 36; (2) Hicks never calls Zeno a 'merchant'. He only had a cargo of purple dye, so I dropped the word; (3) the draft's 'followed him for years' meaning was loose, because he left Crates and the twenty years were spread over several teachers. Meaning line changed to match. Zeno is not on the used list. The used entry 'Zeno on his student Cleanthes' is a different passage.
kept.safety: Safe as written. Leave out these nearby parts: the shipwreck (VII.2, no victims, but it is a disaster), the oracle telling him to 'take on the complexion of the dead' (VII.2), Crates smashing the soup pot with his staff (VII.3), and Zeno's death (VII.28). No war, royalty or politics in the trimmed story.

kept.who: Democritus · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers IX.35-36, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb), 1925
kept.corrected_who: Democritus (c. 460-370 BCE) · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers IX.35-36, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb vol. II), 1925
kept.corrected_quote: Democritus took his share of the family property in money, "because he had need of this to pay the cost of travel," and spent it all, learning geometry from priests in Egypt and, some say, visiting India's wise men.
kept.corrected_meaning: He spent all his family money travelling far to learn from wise teachers.
kept.evidence: Opened the Wikisource raw text of Hicks, Book IX. IX.35: 'he travelled into Egypt to learn geometry from the priests, and he also went into Persia to visit the Chaldaeans as well as to the Red Sea. Some say that he associated with the Gymnosophists in India and went to Aethiopia. Also that, being the third son, he divided the family property. Most authorities will have it that he chose the smaller portion, which was in money, because he had need of this to pay the cost of travel.' IX.36: 'Demetrius estimates his share at over 100 talents, the whole of which he spent.' IX.39 adds that he came home from his travels having 'exhausted his means'. The quoted fragment is word for word, and India stays labelled 'some say'. Fix: the draft ran 45 words, now 39. I dropped the vague 'then Persia' (in DL that means visiting the Chaldaeans). Not on the used list.

Leave out: King Xerxes and his Magi (IX.34), the ox brought for sacrifice (IX.36), him 'frequenting tombs' (IX.38), the law about burying people who wasted their inheritance (IX.39), and the later legend that he blinded himself. kept.corrected_who: Seneca · Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 52.8 ('On choosing our teachers'), tr. Richard M. Gummere (Loeb vol. I), 1917
kept.corrected_quote: Choose as a guide one whom you will admire more when you see him act than when you hear him speak.

kept.who: Antisthenes · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI.2, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb), 1925
kept.corrected_who: Antisthenes (c. 445-365 BCE) · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI.2, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb vol. II), 1925
kept.corrected_quote: Antisthenes had pupils of his own, yet he became Socrates's pupil and told them to join him. Living at the port of Peiraeus, he "every day would tramp the five miles to Athens in order to hear Socrates."
kept.corrected_meaning: Already a teacher, he became a student again and walked about 8 km to class every day.
kept.evidence: Opened the Wikisource raw text of Hicks, Book VI. VI.2: 'To begin with, he became a pupil of Gorgias the rhetorician... Later on, however, he came into touch with Socrates, and derived so much benefit from him that he used to advise his own disciples to become fellow-pupils with him of Socrates. He lived in the Peiraeus, and every day would tramp the five miles to Athens in order to hear Socrates.' The quoted part is word for word. Yonge's translation (Fordham sourcebook) gives 'forty furlongs', which supports the Greek 'forty stadia', about 7.4 km. Hicks's 'five miles' is about 8 km, and the meaning line follows Hicks. DL gives the distance only for the walk to Athens, so 'about 8 km to class' is correct and I made no claim about the walk back. Fix: the draft ran 46 words, now 37. Not on the used list.
kept.safety: Safe as trimmed. Leave out: the battle of Tanagra and the taunt about his Thracian mother (VI.1), and the same section's 'Heracles and Cyrus' example (Cyrus was a king). I did not check the Eudoxus backup (VIII.86) and am not returning it here.

kept.who: Aeschines of Sphettus (pupil of Socrates) · Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis) I.8, tr. Aubrey Stewart (Bohn's Classical Library), 1887
kept.corrected_who: Aeschines of Sphettus and Socrates, an old anecdote told by Seneca, On Benefits (De Beneficiis) I.8, tr. Aubrey Stewart (London: George Bell & Sons, Bohn's Classical Library), 1887
kept.corrected_quote: As Socrates' pupils gave him presents, poor Aeschines said: "...I present you with the only thing I possess, myself." Socrates answered: "...I will accordingly take pains to restore you to yourself a better man than when I received you."
kept.original: Itaque dono tibi, quod unum habeo, me ipsum. ... Habebo itaque curae, ut te meliorem tibi reddam, quam accepi.
kept.corrected_meaning: A poor student had nothing to give, so he gave himself, and the teacher promised to make him better.
kept.evidence: Downloaded Gutenberg #3794 (Title: L. Annaeus Seneca on Benefits, Translator: Aubrey Stewart). Book I, ch. VIII reads: 'As the pupils of Socrates, each in proportion to his means, gave him large presents, Aeschines, a poor pupil, said, "I can find nothing to give you which is worthy of you; I feel my poverty in this respect alone. Therefore I present you with the only thing I possess, myself. ..." Socrates answered, "Surely you have bestowed a great present upon me, unless perchance you set a small value upon yourself. I will accordingly take pains to restore you to yourself a better man than when I received you."' All the quoted words match. Latin checked on thelatinlibrary.com/sen/ben1.shtml [8]: 'Aeschines, pauper auditor ... Itaque dono tibi, quod unum habeo, me ipsum ... Habebo itaque curae, ut te meliorem tibi reddam, quam accepi.' archive.org lists the edition as George Bell & Sons, 1887. What I fixed: the story was about 60 words, so I cut it to 39. I added '...' where 'Therefore' and Socrates' first sentence were cut. Seneca wrote about 400 years after the event (Diogenes Laertius II.34 has a shorter version), so I labelled it an anecdote. Not in used_quotes.txt. Stage 2 fits, since poverty is the obstacle; it could also work as stage 1, giving yourself to the teacher.
kept.safety: Clean as trimmed. Leave out the very next sentence comparing him to Alcibiades, a politician and general. Do not mention Socrates' trial or death. There is no violence, politics or royalty in the quoted part.

kept.who: Diogenes of Sinope · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI.21, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb), 1925
kept.corrected_who: Diogenes of Sinope and Antisthenes, a traditional story (legend; historians doubt they met) · Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI.21, tr. R. D. Hicks (Loeb), 1925
kept.corrected_quote: An old story says Antisthenes turned Diogenes away "because he never welcomed pupils," but "by sheer persistence Diogenes wore him out. ... From that time forward he was his pupil..."
kept.corrected_meaning: The teacher said no, but the student would not give up, and in the end the teacher said yes.
kept.evidence: Fetched the Wikisource raw text of Lives of the Eminent Philosophers/Book VI (translator Robert Drew Hicks). Section 21: 'On reaching Athens he fell in with Antisthenes. Being repulsed by him, because he never welcomed pupils, by sheer persistence Diogenes wore him out. Once when he stretched out his staff against him, the pupil offered his head with the words, "Strike, for you will find no wood hard enough to keep me away from you, so long as I think you've something to say." From that time forward he was his pupil, and, exile as he was, set out upon a simple life.' The quoted fragments match exactly. kept.evidence: Russian Wikisource, Dal 'Пословицы русского народа', section 'Ученье — Наука', prints: 'Век живи — век учись (а умри дураком).' The same section has 'Не выучит школа, выучит охота.' and 'Не выучит школа — выучит охота (нужда).', and also 'Ученье — свет, а неученье — тьма.' I found no 'стыдно не учиться' line in that section. Gummere's Letter 76 (English Wikisource page scan, IA adlucilium02sene, p. 149), §3 reads: 'You should keep learning as long as you are ignorant,—even to the end of your life, if there is anything in the proverb. And the proverb suits the present case as well as any: "As long as you live, keep learning how to live."' The trim with '...' is faithful. The Latin at thelatinlibrary.com (ep. 76.3) reads: 'Tamdiu discendum est quamdiu nescias; si proverbio credimus, quamdiu vivas. Nec ulli hoc rei magis convenit quam huic: tamdiu discendum est quemadmodum vivas quamdiu vivas.' The candidate's trimmed Latin matches. Only fix: the meaning line said 'Even 2,000 years ago'. Seneca wrote c. 64-65 CE, so I changed it to 'Almost 2,000 years ago'. Seneca calls it 'the proverb', so I wrote 'already said this as a proverb' and dropped the guess 'old'. Neither line is in the used list (the used Russian lines are different proverbs, and the used Seneca lines are Letters 2 and 104).
kept.safety: Print only the first half of the Russian proverb, not '(а умри дураком)'. Dal also files it under 'Жизнь — Смерть'. Letter 76 is titled 'On learning wisdom in old age', and its §§1-3 mention an old man, the arena and duels. Use only the trimmed lines, and do not show the letter's title on the slide (no old-age lines). Do not quote the next sentence, 'That even an old man should keep learning.'

kept.corrected_who: Luo Congyan (1072-1135) · as recorded in the History of Song (Song Shi, completed 1345), juan 428 (Daoxue 2), biography of Luo Congyan · translation ours
kept.corrected_quote: Luo Congyan walked to study with Yang Shi, and after three days said, "Had I not come here, I would almost have lived my life in vain." Later he sold his fields to ask Cheng Yi in Luoyang.
kept.original: 聞同郡楊時得河南程氏學，慨然慕之……遂徒步往學焉。……從彥初見時三日，即驚汗浹背，曰：「不至是，幾虛過一生矣。」……從彥即鬻田走洛，見頤問之……乃歸卒業。
kept.corrected_meaning: He walked to find his teacher and sold his land to learn more. His will to learn never stopped.
kept.evidence: Opened zh.wikisource 宋史/卷428, 羅從彥 section. Every Chinese fragment is there verbatim: 聞同郡楊時得河南程氏學，慨然慕之，及時為蕭山令，遂徒步往學焉 … 從彥初見時三日，即驚汗浹背，曰：「不至是，幾虛過一生矣。」 … 從彥即鬻田走洛，見頤問之，頤反覆以告，從彥謝曰：「聞之龜山具是矣。」乃歸卒業. The quoted speech is documented. 惟從彥可與言道 is also there. CBDB (person 25127) gives 1072-1135. The candidate's story text was about 70 words, so I shortened it to 38 words in 2 sentences. 'Came home to finish his studies with Yang' is an interpretation; the text only says 乃歸卒業 (returned and finished his studies). Correction to the notes: the biography says he did hold a minor clerk post, 惠州博羅縣主簿, obtained by repeated exam grace, before he 絕意仕進 (gave up seeking office). So 'kept away from office' is only partly true. Leave it out anyway. Dating: Yang Shi's Xiaoshan post is usually dated 1112 (政和), after Cheng Yi died in 1107, so the Song Shi's order may be unreliable. Tell it as 'the History of Song records', with no years and no Xiaoshan. Not in the used list.
kept.safety: The trimmed story is safe. The rest of the biography covers politics, court officials, rebellions (Lushan, Zhu Ci) and the Jingkang 'national calamity'. Do not use any of it. Leave out Luo's clerk post and Yang Shi's official posts.

kept.corrected_who: Confucius · Analects VII.19 (7.20 in some numberings, e.g. D. C. Lau) · tr. James Legge, The Chinese Classics vol. 1, 1861 (rev. 1893)
kept.corrected_quote: I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge; I am one who is fond of antiquity, and earnest in seeking it there.
kept.original: 子曰：「我非生而知之者，好古，敏以求之者也。」
kept.corrected_meaning: Even Confucius said he was not born wise. He loved the old teachings and worked hard to find them.
kept.evidence: Opened Gutenberg #3330 (Legge, The Analects, from the Chinese Classics). Book VII, CHAP. XIX reads exactly: 'The Master said, 'I am not one who was born in the possession of knowledge; I am one who is fond of antiquity, and earnest in seeking it there.'' The Chinese matches the standard text. CHAP. VII is also there as given: 'From the man bringing his bundle of dried flesh for my teaching upwards, I have never refused instruction to any one.' Another Stage 3 option is CHAP. VIII: 'I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge...' VII.19 is not in the used list (used: 2.4, 9.19, 11.21, 13.17, 17.2, and Doctrine of the Mean ch. 20). I moved the stage from 'arc' to '3'. The line is about love of learning and earnest seeking (好, 敏, 求). It has no 'it was not easy' beat, so it does not cover the whole journey.
kept.safety: Safe. Do not quote across into VII.18, the line just before, which ends 'does not perceive that old age is coming on' (old-age line) and names the Duke of Sheh (royalty/official).
